A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same OpenNER resource and retain identifiable matching methods and experiments. All pages, figures, tables and appendices are readable, supporting reliable comparison despite substantial expansion and reorganization.

before.justification: v1 Section 5 and Tables 2-3 report original fine-tuning experiments with mBERT, XLM-R and Glot500, including individual and multilingual models and results across random seeds.

after.justification: v2 retains original encoder experiments and reports additional LLM benchmarks, prompting experiments and dataset-quality analyses in Section 4 and the appendices.

M1.justification: The OpenNER construction procedure remains dataset selection, CoNLL/BIO conversion, label-transition repair, entity-type standardization and optional reduction to core types. v2 documents mappings and implementation more explicitly; its LLM additions are benchmark methods, without an established change to the proposed resource-construction procedure.

E1.justification: v2 adds evaluated ArmanPersoNER data in Persian and WNUT17 English emerging-entity web data, expanding OpenNER from 34 corpora and 51 languages to 36 corpora and 52 languages. Appendix A.4 also newly uses CoNLL-03 English for prompting trials, although that corpus remains excluded from the distributed collection.

E2.justification: v1 benchmarks three encoder models. v2 retains them and adds Aya-Expanse 32b and QwQ-32B-Preview to the core-type comparison, with results in Tables 3 and 12. This substantially broadens the comparison to generative LLM approaches.

E3.justification: v2 introduces five-shot in-context evaluation using inline entity output and fixed demonstrations selected per corpus and language. Demonstration selection includes sentence-length and entity-presence controls, and preliminary trials select the prompting format. Retained corpora's splits and the previously stated fine-tuning hyperparameters remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Appendix A.4 adds a small Aya-Expanse study on CoNLL-03 English: JSON output scores 61.46 F1, inline output 67.42, and inline output with five demonstrations 74.86. Appendix B adds targeted annotation-error audits of excluded datasets. These supplement the retained ontology and individual-versus-multilingual comparisons.

E5.justification: Encoder results retain the ten-seed mean and standard-error reporting used in v1. v2 adds three demonstration-selection seeds for LLM evaluations, accompanying uncertainty values in Table 12, and standard errors across dataset-language combinations in Table 3. It does not establish an increase in repetitions of retained individual-model experiments.

E6.justification: Shared individual-model scores are unchanged, but multilingual results are extensively revised: KazNERD multilingual XLM-R changes from 88.68 in v1 Table 3 to 94.11 in v2 Table 6. Expanded multilingual training coverage prevents interpreting this as a matched-setting gain. v2 also adds encoder results for two corpora, LLM results across 67 dataset-language combinations, and prompting-study outcomes.

T1.justification: Neither version develops mathematical theory, formal assumptions, theorems or proofs. The added mapping tables and examples provide technical documentation without introducing new mathematical definitions or derivations.

C1.justification: The standardized multilingual resource remains the central contribution. v2 expands its coverage and benchmark claims, explicitly claims the largest-to-date entity-type standardization, and adds the abstract-level finding that high LLM NER performance remains challenging. The conclusion shifts its stated modeling challenge from handling multiple ontologies to handling multiple languages.

C2.justification: v2 substantially qualifies cross-corpus comparability: identical type names can retain different annotation guidelines, spans and contextual labeling conventions. New limitations address regional, language and script imbalances and incomplete coverage. It also adds tentative explanations involving annotation compatibility and demonstration limitations, while bounding the LLM conclusions to comparatively simple prompting.

D1.justification: v2 adds explicit standardization and core-type mappings, document-boundary handling, encoder-head and subtoken details, parameter counts, hardware and computational costs, and LLM prompt and generation details. The 32k multilingual training cap is newly documented; v1 does not specify a cap. A new footnote states that data, models and software will be released upon publication.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands the research context through LLM-NER work, including llmner, GPT-NER, zero-shot ChatGPT studies, synthetic-data generation and demonstration retrieval. It also adds provenance references for included and audited corpora. The existing distinction from UNER's uniform annotation and silver-standard resources is retained.

P1.justification: Dataset selection is integrated into Data Sources, while much existing corpus and formatting detail moves to Appendices A and C. The introduction and standardization explanations are substantially rewritten, and the narrative gains separate core-type, LLM, discussion, limitations and ethics sections. These changes substantially reorganize existing material as well as accommodate additions.

P2.justification: v2 adds a processing-pipeline figure and tables for dataset sources, mappings, aggregate comparisons, core-type counts, prompts and LLM results. Existing detailed encoder-result tables move into the appendix. The retained performance plots are redrawn with gridlines, revised axis ticks and legends below the plots.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses v1's sparse documentation of the central standardization process and experimental implementation through explicit mappings and Appendix A. Dataset-quality audits and concrete annotation and coverage limitations make the resource more auditable and its results easier to interpret. The LLM benchmarks broaden useful evidence, although reporting issues remain: Table 3's LLM means of 60.55 and 60.66 do not reconcile with Table 12's row averages of approximately 60.43 and 60.47. These small discrepancies do not outweigh the substantial gains in documentation and interpretation.
